newsitem.title: USA: Lack of profits may have hit Dec cattle placements.
newsitem.headline: Lack of profits may have hit Dec cattle placements.

text.p: U.S. cattle feeders in the seven key cattle feeding states placed a smaller number of cattle on feed than expected in December but the low placements may have been linked to a lack of profit potential.

The U.S. Agriculture Department on Friday reported December seven-state placements at 98 percent of a year ago, well below the average trade estimate of 108.2 percent of a year ago and below all estimates of 103 to 112 percent.
Most analysts were unable to give a reason for the discrepancy.
Based on surveys analysts conduct for a base percentage of the largest feedlots, the placement number should have been at least 104 to 105 percent, several analysts said.

But Dave Maher with Securities Corp of Iowa, said he expected the lower placements based on the feedlots he had contacted. The financial position that most feedlots appeared to be in during December and the cost of feed and feeder cattle kept operators from putting cattle on feed, he said.

"Your feeding margins were going to be negative because you can't buy feeder cattle that are going to finish in April and June and have a $63 or $64 (futures) board and be paying $72 to $74 for feeders. A lot of them (cattle feeders) were a little bit more frugal on filling these pens," Maher said.

Because of the low placement number, Chicago Mercantile Exchange live cattle futures were being called higher to sharply higher on Monday. Analysts are looking for live cattle to be 0.250 to 1.000 cent per lb higher with April and June pacing the advance. Feeder cattle futures were also called at least 0.250 to 0.500 cent higher.
Tom Tippens, CEO Professional Cattle Consultants Inc, said he had questions about the placement numbers but said "the fact is, it's official and we'll trade on it for awhile."
One of biggest discrepancies in actual placements versus expectations, came in Colorado.

Maher said many cattle feeders in Colorado are also involved with cow/calf operations and that part of the business was showing a loss. Bankers were unwilling to loan more money to those operators that were in both ends of the business, he said.

The number of cattle on feed as of January 1 as well as December marketings indicated on the report were both in line with expectations. On-feed supplies were put at 103 percent of last year compared with the average estimate of 104.2 percent while marketings were at 100 percent versus the average of analysts' estimates at 101.8.
The marketing number was viewed as neutral to mildly bullish for February cattle futures.
"It's a good number because we marketed all the cattle that were available to be marketed during the month of December," said Chuck Levitt, senior livestock analyst for Alaron Trading Corp.
